title: The Dangerous Idea Rubio and Hegseth Are Endorsing
text:
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. 

 When Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was reprimanded by a sentinel last week for a lack of decorum at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, his response was unusually gracious: He promptly awarded the sentinel the Joint Service Commendation Medal. Perhaps Hegseth’s conciliatory response was not because he recognized he’d violated the sanctity of the location , but because he’d been yelled at by one authority he recognizes: a man with a gun.

 This thought occurred to me over the weekend, when Hegseth posted a clip of Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaking at a Federalist Society conference Friday evening. Rubio praised President Trump’s sanctions earlier this year on the International Criminal Court. So far, so normal: The right has long despised the ICC, arguing that it violates American sovereignty and could be used as a foreign-policy weapon by U.S. adversaries. Then things got strange. Rubio said that if the ICC tried to exercise jurisdiction over Americans, “our answer will probably be the same as the Roman general, Pompey, when he said to those who were trying to invoke their cities’ charters against his legions. He said, ‘Stop quoting laws to men with swords.’”

 This is an odd thing to say to a room full of lawyers, and it was met with some awkward chuckles. Only once Rubio declared Pompey’s statement as “not politically correct” did he win applause. But Hegseth was apparently taken with the quote and reposted it, writing , “Stop quoting laws to MEN WITH SWORDS.”

 Rubio and Hegseth are expressing a core view of the second Trump administration: that might makes right and rules are for sissies. In January, now–White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller explained the American quasi-colonization of Venezuela this way. “We live in a world in which you can talk all you want about international niceties and everything else, but we live in a world,” he said, “that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power. These are the iron laws of the world that have existed since the beginning of time.” (No wonder that the United States—with Rubio acting as viceroy—has signaled that it prefers rule by the Nicolás Maduro protégé Delcy Rodríguez to María Corina Machado’s attempts to restore democracy in the country.) Trump has shown that he prefers the performative machismo of Vladimir Putin’s Russian military to Ukraine’s legal and moral claim on its land, and he has mused publicly about actions against Iran that would be war crimes.

 The Trumpist fidelity to this idea is particularly true with regard to international law, but it extends to a consistent disregard for the laws of the United States as well. At the Pentagon, Hegseth has raged against rules of engagement for the military and loosened them for the war in Iran, which may be one reason that the U.S. bombed an elementary school in Iran early in the conflict. (Superior American military might has not prevailed in Iran so far, either.) The military has also killed almost 250 people in extrajudicial and likely illegal strikes on boats that American officials allege are carrying drugs.

 The epithet un-American is overused, but in this case, it is literally true. “The very purpose of the American founding was to ensure that force would always be subject to law, which would itself flow from natural right and popular consent,” John R. Puri writes in National Review . “That is why one of the Founders’ great innovations was to place the new U.S. armed forces under strict civilian control.” One specific complaint in the Declaration of Independence was that King George III had “affected to render the Military independent of and superior to the Civil power.” By contrast, John Adams wrote that a republic was a government “of Laws, and not of Men,” a stipulation that very much includes men with swords who might try to supersede law.

 Hegseth is himself now a lawless man with (metaphorical) swords, and in his enthusiastic endorsement of Rubio’s remark, we may find insight into both why Hegseth joined the Army out of college and why his career languished. Maybe he thought joining the military was a ticket to cracking heads without restriction. Instead, he found a careful, disciplined, and rule-abiding force, and he never advanced very far. As my colleague Eliot A. Cohen has written , “The Army, unlike Princeton and Harvard, knew a petulant, insecure mediocrity when it saw one.” Hegseth eventually left the National Guard when he was sidelined over concerns about extremism. As secretary, he has gone about destroying the institution that spurned him, as well as working to ensure that the people bearing swords are almost entirely men.

 As for Rubio, he has recently become a fount of classical references , perhaps under the influence of white-nationalist ideas circulating at the State Department. But mouthing these words is different from understanding what they mean. As a young commander during a Roman civil war in the 80s B.C.E., Pompey earned the nickname adulescentulus carnifex —“teenage butcher.” When residents of the Sicilian city of Messana resisted his authority, citing ancient Roman law, he uttered the quotation that Rubio cites. The American Founders—and indeed most Americans throughout history—would have seen themselves in the citizens of Messana, not the ruthless general.

 Things didn’t turn out well for Pompey. He enjoyed years of political and military success during a period when republican rule was teetering, eventually becoming part of a ruling triumvirate with Julius Caesar and Marcus Licinius Crassus. But he eventually fell out with Caesar, resulting in another civil war. Pompey fled Rome but was killed and beheaded in Egypt. Nor, more important, did Pompey’s era end well for the Roman Republic. When the long-running political crisis that spawned both civil wars was over, the republic was dead, and Rome was ruled by an emperor.

 It is possible—even probable—that the Trump figures quoting Pompey do not know this history. But understanding it is not necessary to grasp why Pompey’s words are nothing to emulate, nor to predict what will happen to a republic that allows such leaders to reach and maintain power.

 Today’s News 

 The Trump administration announced a new rule restricting Chinese companies’ access to advanced American AI chips through overseas data centers, closing a loophole in U.S. export controls. The rule, which takes effect in 90 days, comes amid tensions within the administration over chip restrictions ahead of President Trump’s planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

 Trump defended his two-day silence on Friday’s nationwide air-traffic shutdown , saying that he had managed the crisis from the White House while leaving public updates to Cabinet officials.

 Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother charged with killing her three young children in 2023, is scheduled to face a second trial beginning March 29, 2027 , after her first trial ended with a hung jury. Prosecutors are expected to pursue first-degree-murder charges again, while Clancy’s defense argues that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible.

 Evening Read

 Awesome

 By Adrienne LaFrance 

 In Jules Verne’s wildest imagination, the technology that would send humanity starward was already familiar on Earth. The launching mechanism for the American rocket, in Verne’s 1865 novel From the Earth to the Moon , is—of all things—a colossal cannon. The speed required to reach the lunar surface, he reasoned, would require a gunshot of a launch. So in Vernian terms, a starship was not merely launched but “fired” into space.

 I’ve been thinking of Verne today as I watched the video (then watched it again, and again) of SpaceX’s latest history-making maneuver. Yesterday, for the first time ever, engineers successfully pulled off a midair landing —using the company’s Mechazilla tower’s “chopstick” arms to snatch a starship the size of a skyscraper out of the sky after it had spent the past 22 hours in Earth’s orbit. Up until this point, Mechazilla’s chopsticks had caught boosters after launch—that is, the part of the rocket that detaches—but never ships themselves.
